sections.title_en: 1. You Shall Not Walk in Their Statutes
sections.body_en:
Modesty is one of the foundations of Judaism. The general command in the Torah (Vayikra 19:2), "You shall be holy," Rashi explains: "Be separate from forbidden relations and from transgression, for wherever you find a fence against forbidden relations you find holiness." And it is further said regarding the prohibition of forbidden relations (ibid. 18:24): "Do not defile yourselves with any of these, for with all these the nations were defiled."

There is a connection between keeping modesty and the excellence of the people of Israel in the realms of the spirit. Even when we were enslaved to the Egyptian nation, of which the Sages said (Torat Kohanim, Aḥarei, ch. 9) that there was no nation as steeped in lewd desire and forbidden relations as the Egyptian nation, we were not swept along after their customs and we kept modesty; and out of that keeping of modesty we merited to stand before Mount Sinai and receive the Torah from Heaven.

Many think superficially that the aim of modest dress is to prevent impure thoughts in men, but the subject is more complex and deep. For there is no chance of preventing every such thought, and the Sages already said (Ketubot 13b): "There is no guardian against forbidden relations." That is, no one can be assured that he is completely protected from it. And if the supreme aim were to prevent such thoughts, they would have had to set much stricter rules: to forbid men to go out into the street without absolute necessity, to forbid drinking wine and other things that release the emotions, to forbid wearing clothes of attractive cut, and likewise to forbid beautiful combinations of colours, to decree that women considered especially beautiful should not go out into the street without necessity, and perhaps to oblige all women to wrap themselves in a large and ugly coat. Yet we find in halakha no demand that a woman make herself ugly. On the contrary, we find in the Tanakh and in the Sages that it is praiseworthy for a woman to be beautiful and to care for her appearance.1

So the laws of modesty were not meant to make beauty ugly or to hide it, but to give it a modest framework that will emphasise the spirit and good qualities. There is in these laws no opposition to the material, physical sides of our lives. On the contrary, every realm has value and a place. But one who does not keep modesty sins, against his will, by over-emphasising materiality over spirituality, the body over the soul. For spirituality is by its nature hidden, and in order to grasp the nature of the soul, the body must be put in its proper place and not emphasised and made into the main thing. Only after spirituality stands in its central place can one look modestly at the physical sides of our lives and draw from them the full force of life, without this harming the soul.

That is, immodesty emphasises the physical, material sides of a person, whereas modesty emphasises the spiritual, soulful foundation of a person. It may be that in the short term it seems as if immodesty helps to reveal the force of life; but one who looks more deeply and over the longer term understands that it is precisely modesty that reveals the inner force of life, holiness, and out of this the material sides of life too are blessed and elevated. It is important to know that as a rule the idea of modesty obligates men too (SA OḤ 2:1-2); but since women are considered more beautiful and men are aroused more quickly, so that they will be able to court their wives, the rules of modesty are stricter regarding women.

Since a person's clothing is prominent and visible to every onlooker, keeping the bounds of the laws of modesty expresses more than anything faithfulness to halakha; and a woman who dresses according to halakha sanctifies the Name and declares at all times: I am not dragged after the culture of the nations and after their fashions, but I am completely faithful to the tradition of Torah and mitzvot and to the special Divine destiny of the people of Israel.

notes_en.en: The Torah mentioned in praise of our mothers Sara, Rivka and Raḥel that they were beautiful. Ta'anit 31a; Ketubot 59b – "A woman is only for beauty"; Yevamot 63b, "A beautiful woman – happy is her husband, the number of his days is doubled"; Nedarim 66a: "Rabbi Yishmael wept and said: The daughters of Israel are beautiful, but poverty makes them unsightly." And part of the festival joy of women is that they wear beautiful clothes and jewellery, and the intention is not that she adorn herself with them only in the company of women.

sections.title_en: 2. The General Prohibitions in Immodesty
sections.body_en:
Three fundamental prohibitions stand at the basis of the laws of modesty.
Or in other words, on the basis of three of the foundations of the Torah one must be careful about the laws of modesty.

First, immodesty is a personal sin: a sin of emphasising the outward sides of a person over the inner sides, making matter stand out over spirit. Before the sin of the first man, Adam and Ḥava walked naked in the Garden of Eden, for the evil inclination had not yet entered them, and there was no flaw in this. But after the appearance of the evil inclination, man became limited, and every excessive exposure of the body constitutes an injury to his spiritual foundation, since there is in it an emphasis of matter over spirit. And every injury to the main sides of a person, that is, to the soul and the spirit, causes a general impoverishment of a person's vitality, something expressed among other things in harm to the capacity to go deeply into spiritual matters, and likewise in the capacity to maintain a marriage in holiness, love and joy. Go and see the immodest actors and singers, who are not able to persist in their love for their spouses; apparently making outwardness stand out prevents them from reaching the inner and deep layers of love.

The second foundation of the prohibition of immodesty is the harm to the wholeness of the family. Severe immodesty usually shatters the family. But even lack of modesty, even slight, harms the family. Love should be directed to one's spouse, for only with him can love appear completely, and every loss of the power of love towards other people is at the expense of developing love within the home, something that harms both the spouse and the children and their education. A woman who tries to attract attention with an immodest appearance is not whole in her love for her husband, and likewise a man who tries to attract the attention of other women is not whole in his love for his wife. By contrast, keeping modesty directs the powers of love to their proper place. In order to create a modest framework, which creates an honourable distance between men and women and distances a person from sin, the Sages set fences for modesty. And so we find in practice that the more correctly people are careful about modesty, the more the chance of marrying and of keeping the wholeness of the family grows. Of course every rule has exceptions, and sometimes modesty stems from a psychological problem and from a lack of love of life. But as a rule it is clear that in a group that is less careful about the laws of modesty, the percentage of single men and women, of divorced men and women, is higher.

The third foundation of modesty is keeping our special national character. For the difference between Israel and the nations has always been expressed in keeping modesty, and to this the Torah prohibition "and you shall not walk in their statutes" (Vayikra 18:3) is directed; its essence is not to imitate the gentiles in clothes that are not modest and in customs connected to superstitions (Maharik, shoresh 88). The quality of modesty, imprinted in the Jewish people through its generations, was the foundation for all the mighty spiritual achievements of the people of Israel, and immodesty by contrast blurs the special virtues and qualities of the Jewish nation.

sections.title_en: 3. Local Custom
sections.body_en:
One of the central questions in the laws of modesty of dress is whether there are absolute rules in the laws of modesty that do not depend on local custom, or whether all the laws of modesty are relative and depend on local custom.

This question will be significant in a place where most women are accustomed to go in summer without sleeves and with short skirts: can one say that, since this is the prevailing custom in that place, the women who live there will be permitted to go in these short clothes, because in the eyes of the society in that place these clothes are considered decent clothes that do not attract special attention, and only one who wears clothes shorter than is accepted will be considered to be transgressing the rules of modesty? Or are there fixed rules in the laws of modesty that depend neither on place nor on time?

Answer: Admittedly there is a view among the poskim that holds that the rules of modesty are determined according to what is accepted in that place and that time (Divrei Ḥamudot on the Rosh, Berakhot 3:37, s.k. 116). But all the other poskim disagreed and established that there are places on a woman's body that must be covered, and even if all the women in that place decide to go in the street without clothes, their custom will be contrary to halakha. For the Sages established that there are places on the body that it is fitting should be covered and kept in purity for the sake of the true love between the couple, and there are places that may be uncovered. And although perhaps if all women go with sleeveless blouses, the sight of a woman without sleeves will cause fewer feelings, nevertheless according to halakha this is not desirable; on the contrary, one should preserve the natural and original sensitivity, which is meant to deepen our feelings and strengthen the love between husband and wife.

To return to the halakha: there are places on the body that must be covered, as will be explained further on, and local custom has no influence regarding them. And there are places that by law there is no obligation to cover, but if all the women who walk there, including women visiting there, are accustomed to cover them, their custom will obligate all the women in that place.

sections.title_en: 4. The Upper Arm
sections.body_en:
In tractate Ketubot (72b) it is explained that a woman must cover her upper arms, and if she uncovers them in public, she is considered to be transgressing dat Yehudit (Jewish custom of modesty). And the rest of the arm that is not the upper arm need not be covered. It is worth noting that in the view of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman (Bereshit Rabba 80:4), the whole episode with Dina began from her upper arm being uncovered in public before Shekhem son of Ḥamor, and out of this he desired her and sinned with her; and from the uncovering of the upper arm the whole calamity told in the Torah followed (Bereshit chapter 34).

But one must clarify where exactly the zero'a (upper arm) is. In the view of most poskim, the zero'a is the part of the arm between the shoulder and the elbow, and according to halakha it must be covered. But what is beyond the elbow, towards the hand, need not be covered. And some are stringent and hold that it is right for a woman to take care to go with a long sleeve down to the hand, either because the zero'a extends to the beginning of the hand, or because in their view this was the custom among women and one should not depart from it (see Beit Barukh vol. 1 p. 101).

In practice, the halakha follows the view of most poskim, who obligate covering up to and including the elbow, and beyond that there is no halakhic obligation to cover (MB 75:2; Halikhot Bat Yisrael p. 70). And as we learned in the previous halakha, in this matter custom has no weight; and even if all the women of a certain place become accustomed to go in a short sleeve that does not reach the elbow, their custom will be considered a custom one should not be drawn after. But from the elbow to the end of the arm the law depends on local custom: by law there is no obligation to wear a sleeve that covers what is beyond the elbow; but if in a certain place all the women are accustomed to go in a long sleeve, their custom will be halakhically binding, and any woman who breaks their custom will be considered a woman who does not keep the rules of modesty.

sections.title_en: 5. May One Uncover Less Than a Tefaḥ?
sections.body_en:
In continuation of the previous halakha it is fitting to mention that some hold that there is no obligation to cover with a sleeve up to and including the elbow, but in their view one may be slightly lenient in this. And since this discussion is important, we will mention the source of their reasoning. In the Talmud (Berakhot 24a) a statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak is brought: "A tefaḥ (handbreadth) in a woman is erva," and its meaning is that a woman may not uncover before strange men more than a tefaḥ of the places that the Sages established she must cover. Accordingly they wanted to conclude that there is no prohibition to uncover less than a tefaḥ of the covered places, and consequently there is no obligation that the sleeve reach past the elbow; rather it is enough that it reach to a distance of less than a tefaḥ from the end of the elbow, and a tefaḥ is about eight centimetres (Hatznea Lekhet p. 139). And since there is such reasoning, one can judge favourably a woman whose sleeve does not reach quite past the elbow but only close to it.

However, according to the vast majority of poskim there is no permission to uncover even less than a tefaḥ of a place that must be covered. And what they said in the Talmud, 'a tefaḥ', is only with regard to saying holy words: if less than a tefaḥ of the covered places is uncovered, it does not have the law of erva, which forbids saying holy words before it; but with regard to the laws of modesty, even less than a tefaḥ must be covered. Further, in the view of the Rema (SA OḤ 75:1), only regarding a man's own wife did they say that less than a tefaḥ is not considered erva; but with another woman, even the uncovering of less than a tefaḥ of the covered places is considered erva before which one may not say holy words, and certainly there is a prohibition to expose it (see Gan Na'ul p. 33).

And so it was ruled in practice: a woman should wear a blouse with sleeves that reach beyond the elbow, so that with every movement she makes, the upper arm, including the elbow, will remain covered.

Seemingly, at first glance, it appears to an outsider who does not know the halakha and its reasons that modesty comes to diminish and limit the force of life. But the aim of modesty is to sanctify life, to release it from the limitation and the ugliness of matter, and thereby to elevate life and increase its power. Modesty does not come to harm love but to increase it.

Keeping modesty not only prevents a person from the sin of forbidden relations and from harming the wholeness of the family, but is also an expression of the holiness of a person's life, and helps him rise to the sanctified values of life. Immodesty emphasises the material and outward side of a person, whereas modesty directs attention to the inner self, to the soul.

sections.title_en: 6. The Length of the Dress and Whether Stockings Are Required
sections.body_en:
In the Talmud (Berakhot 24a) a statement of Rav Ḥisda is brought: "The shok in a woman is erva." That is, the shok is one of the intimate places, whose exposure to the eyes of strange men is considered immodesty, and one may not say holy words facing an uncovered shok.

In the view of most poskim, the shok is the part between the knee and the ankle, and if so one must cover the leg down to the ankle. But there is no need to cover the whole leg specifically with a dress; rather it is enough that the dress reach past the knee, and below that one wears socks or tights. It is important to emphasise that tights help only for covering the lower part of the leg, between the knee and the ankle, but will not help for covering the thighs, which modesty requires to be covered by a dress or a skirt. So hold most poskim (Baḥ; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 75:1; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 75:3; Ḥazon Ish 16:8; Minḥat Yitzḥak 6:10; Rav Tzvi Yehuda).

But in the view of one of the great later poskim, the author of the important commentary on the 'Shulḥan Arukh', part 'Oraḥ Ḥayim' – the 'Mishna Berura' (75:2) – the shok is the upper part of the leg, and it ends at the knee, and it is what we call the thigh. And consequently, if the shok ends at the knee, there is no obligation to cover what is below the knee, neither by a dress nor by tights. And although the author of the 'Mishna Berura' is in a minority position, since his rulings were accepted in Israel, many women follow him. But certainly at the very least, even according to the lenient view of the author of the 'Mishna Berura', one must wear a dress that reaches beyond the knee, so that in every position the knee will remain covered (see Gan Na'ul 37; Halikhot Bat Yisrael 71).

Question: A daughter whose parents' household custom is to be careful to wear stockings, and her parents ask her to continue their custom – must she obey them, or may she rely on the view of the 'Mishna Berura' and be lenient?

Answer: She should act as they do and wear stockings; and beyond this being the view of most poskim, there are two further reasons for it: a) It is part of the mitzva of honouring parents to treat them with respect and to obey them, at least while living in their home. Admittedly, when parents tell a person to act contrary to halakha, one may not obey them (SA YD 240:15; above 1:15; 1:20). But when parents ask to act according to the view of most poskim, one must obey them. b) We have already mentioned that even according to the lenient view, in a place where it is customary to cover the shok and the foot, they must be covered. And a daughter who lives in a family whose daughters are careful to cover the leg with stockings is considered, in a certain respect, as one who lives in a place where it is customary to cover, and she must cover.

And although it is fitting for the daughter to continue her custom also after her marriage, nevertheless, if after her marriage she wants to be lenient in this, since she no longer lives in their home, she may, for she has on whom to rely.

sections.title_en: 7. Young Girls
sections.body_en:
A question that is important to clarify in the laws of modesty is from what age one must take care that girls keep the laws of modesty.

Some say that the matter does not depend on age; rather, once the girl already looks somewhat grown and is approaching adolescence, at about ten or eleven, she must be careful about all the laws of modesty. But the Sages did not obligate young girls in the laws of modesty. For the purpose of the laws of modesty is to fence a person off from transgression and from thoughts of transgression; and therefore as long as the girls are young and desire does not govern the sight of them, they need not be particular about the laws of modesty. But when the daughter begins to approach adolescence, she must be careful about all the laws of modesty. And there is no fixed age for this, because the matter varies from girl to girl (Ḥazon Ish OḤ 16:8). However, it is important to note that all this is from the aspect of the obligation of modesty; but from the aspect of the mitzva of education, one must educate every girl to dress as halakha requires from the time she reaches the age of education, which is about six.

And some say that just as regarding the prohibitions of yiḥud one must take care that a strange man not be secluded alone with a girl from the age of three, so the law is regarding all the laws of modesty, and one must take care to buy a girl, already from the age of three, long dresses that reach beyond the knee and blouses with sleeves that pass the elbow (MB, Bei'ur Halakha 75:1, s.v. 'tefaḥ').

In practice it is customary to rule that one should educate daughters in modest dress from the age of education, which is about six. And from the time they approach adolescence one must be careful about this by the law of modesty itself (see Gan Na'ul 44; Halikhot Bat Yisrael 67).

sections.title_en: 8. Trousers for Women
sections.body_en:
In recent generations the question arose whether women may wear trousers. The problem is made up of two parts:
a) From the aspect of the prohibition of 'lo yilbash', as it is said (Devarim 22:5): "A man's garment shall not be on a woman, nor shall a man wear a woman's garment, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God."
b) From the aspect of modesty.
We will briefly survey the two problems.

First, in the view of several poskim, among them the author of the responsa 'Minḥat Yitzḥak' (2:108), trousers are defined as men's clothing; and therefore even if many women become accustomed to wear trousers, and even if there are prominent differences between men's trousers and women's trousers, trousers will still be considered a distinctly male garment, and women will be forbidden to wear them. Moreover, according to this view, since from the outset women were forbidden to wear trousers, consequently one does not take into account that today many women are accustomed to wear them, because their custom is founded on error and transgression.

But in the view of many poskim, if many women become accustomed to wear trousers, or if there is a significant difference between men's trousers and women's trousers, the prohibition of 'lo yilbash' will not exist regarding those trousers. For the prohibition of 'lo yilbash' exists only regarding clothes that are defined as clothes of the other sex, and women's trousers are not defined as men's clothes. Therefore a woman who wants on cold days to wear trousers under her skirt to warm her legs will not be transgressing the prohibition of 'lo yilbash' (Responsa Avnei Tzedek 72; Darkhei Teshuva YD 182:9; and so it is implied by the Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 12:10; SA YD 182:5; Baḥ there). However, it may be that even in their view a woman may wear women's trousers only in places where there are no men, but to go out into the street with women's trousers is forbidden also from the aspect of the prohibition of 'lo yilbash', because going out into the street in trousers is still considered a men's custom. Indeed, to this day, even among the secular public, the sign for women is a figure in a skirt and for men a figure in trousers.

But all this is only from the aspect of the prohibition of 'lo yilbash'; even if this prohibition does not exist regarding women's trousers, nevertheless from the aspect of the obligation of modesty women may not wear trousers. For the aim of modesty is to hide and blur the parting of the legs; and therefore out of the natural sense of modesty women have been accustomed from days of old to wear dresses and skirts and not trousers, for trousers make the parting of the legs stand out, whereas the dress blurs it.

According to halakha, most poskim forbid trousers only because of modesty; therefore in a place where there is no harm to modesty, there is no prohibition in wearing trousers. For example, a woman who wants to wear pyjama trousers at night: since this is done inside her home, there is no problem of modesty and it is permitted. And likewise women who want to exercise in a closed place may wear tracksuit trousers. And likewise women who wish may wear trousers under a dress in winter, in order to warm their legs. And it is good to take care that the trousers not be seen below the dress, so that it will be clear that they are meant for warmth. But if they are seen below the dress, there is a concern of the prohibition of 'lo yilbash' according to some of the poskim, and there is also a concern that this will cause a stumbling block, lest after wearing trousers they will not wear a long enough skirt.

At the same time it is important to know that if there is a woman who is not interested in being careful about all the bounds of halakha, but on the other hand it is important to her to know the guidance of halakha regarding keeping modesty, and she asks what is preferable – a short skirt that does not reach the knee, or wide and relatively modest women's trousers – the answer is that one should prefer the trousers, whose prohibition is relatively light, over the short skirt that does not reach the knee, whose prohibition is more severe (Gan Na'ul p. 45, in the name of Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook zt"l).

Question: May women wear trousers under a dress?

Answer: If the trousers are meant for warmth or for additional modesty, as was the custom in Yemen, it is permitted. But if they wear a dress that is not so long, and their intention is that the trousers be seen below the dress for beauty, it is forbidden, because trousers are considered a man's garment, and a woman may not wear them in order to beautify herself with them.

sections.title_en: 9. A Red Garment and General Rules of Modesty
sections.body_en:
Some say that one may not wear a red garment, because it is the way of the gentiles to wear red clothes (Beit Yosef and Rema, YD 178, in the name of the Maharik, shoresh 88). But the Maharik explains that the fact that the gentiles are accustomed to wear a certain garment does not forbid it to us; only if that garment expresses an idolatrous belief or immodesty does the prohibition "and you shall not walk in their statutes" (Vayikra 18:3) apply to wearing it. And since the colour red expresses, more than all the colours, immodesty and pride, therefore there is a prohibition to wear red clothes as the gentiles wear them.

It may be that the reason the colour red is considered among the gentiles a colour symbolising immodesty is that it is the colour of blood, and consequently also the colour of the internal organs and of the intimate places of the body. And by wearing a red garment they wanted to make stand out outwardly, with brazenness and immodesty, the intimate sides that by nature are covered and hidden. In addition, the colour red alludes to murder and bloodshed (and it is the colour of Edom; see Ramban, Vayikra 16:8).

But some Aḥaronim hold that today there is no prohibition to wear red clothes, because in their view the prohibition of following their custom applies only when the gentiles were accustomed to go in red clothes; but since today there is no distinct custom of gentiles to go in red clothes, there is no prohibition in it. And so ruled one of the great poskim who lived more than a hundred years ago, the gaon Rabbi Yitzḥak Elḥanan of Kovno (see Darkhei Teshuva 178, s.k. 16).

In summary, in the view of many poskim even today there is a prohibition to wear red clothes. And the prohibition is when the whole garment or most of it is conspicuously red; but a garment only a minority of which is coloured red is permitted according to all the poskim. And likewise it is permitted according to all the poskim to wear a garment whose colour is not really red, such as pink or burgundy. And some poskim are lenient in our time to wear even an entirely red garment; those who wish to be lenient have on what to rely, and ideally it is fitting to follow the view of the stringent.

Here is the place to explain that the fundamental rule of the laws of modesty is not to attract excessive attention. This rule is true for every person, men and women alike. Therefore it is not enough to keep the outward bounds of halakha, for a woman can keep outwardly all the laws of modesty and yet her dress and behaviour will not be modest. However, within the framework of a modest appearance, there is nothing wrong with a woman looking beautiful; on the contrary, it is fitting for every young woman and woman to care for her appearance and to express her beauty. But this beauty should be gentle and somewhat inward, conveying pleasantness, faithfulness and kind-heartedness, and not a beauty that attracts sexually and conveys provocation and showiness.

sections.title_en: 10. A Woman's Singing Voice
sections.body_en:
In the Talmud (Berakhot 24a) the words of the Amora Shmuel are brought: "A woman's voice is erva." And the intention is not to the voice of speech but specifically to the voice of song, because the voice of song reveals the depths of the soul more than the voice of speech; and it is among the bounds of modesty that strange men should not hear a woman singing.

It is fitting to repeat the important foundation that all the laws dealing with the details of modesty stem from the special esteem that halakha has for love, on which the whole world is founded, and their aim is to keep all the things that can arouse desire directed to strengthening the bond and love between the couple. And all the fences of modesty are meant to hedge these deep powers so that they will not sweep a person outside the straight and proper circle of life. This is also the reason for the Sages' ruling that a woman's voice is erva. If so, the intention is not to say that there is anything shameful in a woman's singing voice; on the contrary, precisely because of the deep side that her singing voice reveals, there is a concern that if she sings in the presence of strange men, an excessive closeness will be created between them that may create an undesirable bond; and therefore the Sages forbade a man to hear the voice of another woman. This law is part of the whole body of the laws of modesty, which are meant to set bounds for creating a modest way of life that keeps an honourable distance between men and women.

Admittedly some hold that there is no prohibition to hear a woman's singing, but only to say holy words while hearing a woman's singing. But in the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, a man may not hear a woman's singing, because of modesty.

And some want to argue that since today hearing the voices of female singers has become widespread through electronic devices, as long as the singer is dressed modestly and sings in a dignified manner, her singing does not arouse impure thoughts, and consequently there is no prohibition in it. But in the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, in any case it is forbidden because of the bounds of modesty. In addition, even according to the reasoning of the lenient, it is not possible to set the halakha in place, for it is not possible to define where exactly the line passes between a dignified appearance and an immodest one, since the matter depends on many factors, such as the singer's appearance and age, her clothes, the way she stands, her movements, the connecting passages, the number of listeners and their distance from the singer. And as is known, it is a fundamental principle of the enactments of the Sages that their words are not given to measures, for if they were given to measures, they could not be upheld. One can set moral guidance by measures, but not halakhot. It turns out, then, that the Sages' intention was to forbid men to hear a woman singing even in a relatively modest framework. (In halakha 13 we will clarify the law of hearing a female singer through electronic devices.)2

notes_en.en:
Berakhot 24a: "A woman's voice is erva; a tefaḥ in a woman is erva." The accepted explanation is that the obligation of modesty applies both to a tefaḥ of the body in a place that is usually covered and to hearing the voice of a woman's singing. And so wrote the Rosh, Ra'ah, Rid and Riaz on Berakhot there, and so wrote the Semag, Semak and many others.
However, some say that the main meaning of this prohibition is that a man may not say holy words, such as Keri'at Shema, while he hears a woman's singing (Rav Hai Gaon, Rav Yehudai Gaon, Ra'avya 1:76; Hagahot Maimoniyot, Hilkhot Keri'at Shema 3:60). And the Aḥaronim disagree about their view: some understood that in their view there is no prohibition to hear a woman's singing voice (Be'er Sheva; Seridei Esh 1:77), and some of the Aḥaronim understood that they too agree that a man may not hear a woman's singing voice (Gra 75:8; Yad Aharon).
Several Rishonim further wrote that the voice of a woman to whom a man is accustomed is not erva (Yere'im, Hagahot Maimoniyot, Ra'avya, Eshkol and others; Rema 75:3). The Ateret Tzvi 75:6 explained: "But a voice one is accustomed to – even a singing voice, since he is accustomed to her he does not come to desire." This implies that among family members, even if they are not first-degree, such as in-laws, there is no prohibition. By contrast, some understood the words of the Rishonim as intending to permit hearing the voice of speech, which is the voice "one is accustomed to." And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 75:6. And so it appears from MB 75:18.
On the other hand, some wanted to be stringent even in hearing the voice of speech, as explained in Sefer Ha-Me'orot in the name of the Ra'avad, and Orḥot Ḥayim in the name of the Ittur; but their intention is to speech beyond what is customary. And according to most poskim there is no prohibition in the voice of speech.
In summary, in the view of most Rishonim it is forbidden to hear a woman's singing voice because of modesty, and regarding the view of a few of the Rishonim the Aḥaronim disagree. Therefore the Aḥaronim ruled that it is forbidden to hear a woman's singing voice because of modesty (SA EH 21:1; MB 75:17).
In the past it was customary that women would lament and move the public to weeping when they accompanied the dead (Ketubot 46b). However, lamenting is entirely different from singing, and therefore the prohibition does not apply to it (Tiferet Yisrael, Mo'ed Katan 3:9).
Seemingly one should ask: how did the Sages decree not to hear a woman's singing, when it is told of Devora the prophetess that she sang a song to Hashem after her victory over Sisera and Yavin (Shofetim 5:1)? The Ḥida explained that the Shekhina rested upon her, and therefore there was no concern of modesty. And some say that she recited a song, and did not sing it with a melody (Matteh Efrayim). One could further say that indeed there are positive sides to a woman's singing, and therefore by Torah law there is no prohibition in hearing it. But the Torah charged the Sages to make enactments and to make a fence for the Torah. And when the Sages saw that openness between men and women causes problems – so much so that one of the sins on account of which the First Temple was destroyed was forbidden relations – they enacted enactments of modesty, and thereby succeeded in fencing Israel in, until these sins became rare.
The reasoning of the lenient that I mentioned above was written by Rabbi Bigman, and its basis is the reasoning of the Levush (Minhagim, end of OḤ) regarding mixed seating at weddings (see Teḥumin 29, p. 138). And it also relies on the view of those who hold that there is no prohibition of hearing a woman's singing voice other than at the time of saying holy words, which was mentioned at the beginning of the note. Above I explained the reason for the prohibition, which is accepted by the overwhelming majority of the rabbis. And so wrote in practice Rabbi Henkin (Benei Banim 4:7) and Rabbi Yaakov Ariel (Teḥumin 30, p. 212).

sections.title_en: 11. A Ceremony in Which Women Sing
sections.body_en:
Question: A person who takes part in a ceremony at which a female singer or a group of male and female singers appears – may he remain at the ceremony, or must he leave? And what should a soldier at such a ceremony do? And must the girls too leave the ceremony out of solidarity with the boys?

Answer: According to what was explained in the previous halakha, a man may not hear a woman's singing; consequently a man must leave a ceremony at which a woman or women sing, and it is fitting for the girls too to show solidarity with the men and leave with them. And one should not argue that perhaps the singer will be offended, for she is not offended by us but by an enactment of the Sages that we are obligated to keep, and she too must keep Torah and mitzvot. And likewise a soldier must leave any ceremony when a female singer sings in it.

However, in special cases one may rely on the view of the lenient and remain there, while taking care not to enjoy and not to look at the singer. For example, in a case where a rabbi is taking part in a memorial ceremony for a fallen soldier, and there is a concern that if he leaves, the family of the holy soldier will be hurt. Likewise a soldier who fears that he will be severely punished if he leaves, or a soldier in the career army whose leaving will endanger his livelihood, may in a pressing situation remain.3

notes_en.en: In the previous note the sources for the whole topic were explained. And one should add that a man who is in his home and hears a woman's singing voice without intention and without wanting to, has no prohibition in this (Meiri on Berakhot 24a; Ha-Ḥinukh 188; Rabbeinu Yona in Sefer Ha-Yir'a 238). And some say that there is a prohibition in this even though he does not intend it (Eshkol), but if it is hard for him to go to another place, he is under duress (Yere'im; MB 75:17). According to the view of the lenient in this, some of the rabbis, when they were obligated by virtue of their office to take part in memorial ceremonies that included passages of singing by a female singer, were accustomed not to leave during the singer's singing, so as not to offend the bereaved families, but they intended not to enjoy the voice of the singing. But in a place where there was no concern of offence, they left. And some wanted to extend the permission to a situation where army orders establish that all soldiers must take part in official ceremonies at which female singers appear: that so as not to create a confrontation with the commanders, the soldiers may hear the singer while taking care not to look at her and not to enjoy her singing. But it seems that one cannot, on the strength of a private permission meant for certain people in order to prevent offence, cancel the halakha that the Sages established and permit all soldiers to take part in ceremonies in which there is women's singing, with the thought that they are always there against their will and against their mind and direct their hearts not to listen to and enjoy the singing. And the fact that there is an order about this does not make the situation more lenient but more stringent, for it is an order against halakha (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 3:9). Therefore, outside a special case, it is right to be stringent, with a readiness to pay a price for it. And one should not argue that in the army one must compromise, because the truth is the opposite: precisely in the army one must be more stringent, as the Torah commanded to guard against an evil thing precisely in the camp (Devarim 23:10; Peninei Halakha, Ha-Am Ve-Ha-Aretz 4:8). Also from the aspect of the consideration of all Israel it is fitting to act so, for the situation in which the army is run in a secular atmosphere, and religious soldiers feel themselves as guests in the army, causes many of the religious public to stop keeping mitzvot in the army; and in reaction it causes others to prefer the Ḥaredi path and not to enlist in the army. So this situation causes the IDF to lose tens of thousands of soldiers. Therefore the more the religious insist on keeping the character and atmosphere suited to them, the more soldiers the IDF will have, and this is the true unity. Whereas compromise in these matters causes in practice division, in which a large public feels alienated from the IDF.

sections.title_en: 12. May Men and Women Sing Together?
sections.body_en:
Question: Does the prohibition for a man to hear a woman's singing voice apply when the woman sings alone, so that her voice can be heard clearly, or also when a whole group sings together? The question concerns singing at a family Shabbat meal and singing within a youth movement.

Rabbi Weinberg (Seridei Esh 1:77) answered regarding a youth movement that in the view of the vast majority of the poskim it is forbidden, because there is no difference between hearing a group of girls and hearing one girl. For the Sages said (Megilla 21b) that a voice that is dear to a person can be heard even among many voices; consequently, the fact that a whole group sings together does not cancel the singing of each and every one of the girls, and hearing their singing is forbidden. But Rabbi Weinberg added that when he came to Germany he saw that even in the homes of the God-fearing, men and women sang Shabbat songs together, and it is understood from his words that they did so even when guests who were not family members were present. And when he asked about their custom, they answered him that so the righteous gaon Rabbi Azriel Hildesheimer and Rabbi Shimshon Raphael Hirsch had ruled leniently, who were known as understanding and experienced in matters of education. If so, it is fitting to explain the reason for their permission, which is based on the view of several of the great Rishonim who hold that the prohibition of hearing a woman's voice applies only when one intends to enjoy her voice, but when there is no such intention, there is no prohibition. And likewise in the book 'Sedei Ḥemed' (Ma'arekhet Kol) he mentioned the view of a Sephardi rabbi who permitted men and women to sing holy songs together, because in holy songs there is no concern of impure thoughts. If so, since the aim is to sing holy songs and not to enjoy the voices of women, and in addition several women sing together, so that without special attention the listener will not distinguish the voice of a particular woman – the rabbis of Germany permitted men and women to sing holy songs together. And in practice Rabbi Weinberg ruled for the directors of the Yeshurun movement in France to be lenient, because through singing together in the youth movement they would be able to arouse the boys and girls to love of the Torah, the people and the land, and to guard them from assimilation.

But in any case a permission is needed for the specific case, for in an ordinary situation one should follow the view of most poskim, who forbid public singing of men and women together. And only a Torah scholar who knows the situation of those asking can decide the question whether the situation requires leniency in joint singing.

Family members: When only close first-degree family members are at the table, the widespread custom, agreed by all the poskim, is that the daughters too sing, and even solo. But the question is how it is fitting to act when the children marry: may the daughters sing also when in-laws and other second-degree relatives are present?

In many God-fearing families they are accustomed to be stringent, even though this custom causes a reduction in Shabbat songs. And in many families they are accustomed to be lenient, so that the daughters sing together aloud but not solo. And so many rabbis' households are accustomed, and so it was the practice in the home of the Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Frank, and in the home of the Rishon Le-Tziyon, Rabbi Ovadia Yosef. And even families that were accustomed to be stringent, if they want to change their custom, may change it ideally, because they were stringent without knowing that many are lenient.4

notes_en.en:
In the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, even holy songs may not be sung by boys and girls together in a youth movement (Tzitz Eliezer 7:28; 14:7); but it is customary not to be particular about the singing of women that rises from the women's section (the Ḥatam Sofer, ḤM 190, was stringent in this).
Regarding Shabbat songs in a family framework with guests, the basis of the reasoning of the lenient is explained in Seridei Esh 1:77, as he testified that so they were accustomed in the families of the God-fearing and of rabbis in Germany, and it is implied that so they were accustomed even when there were guests, Torah observers, who were not family members. At first I held that the widespread custom is that if there are second-degree relatives there, the women do not sing. But over the years I heard testimonies that even in the homes of rabbis from other communities the custom was that women sang with second-degree family members. Prof. Shaul Stampfer told me that in the home of Rabbi Tzvi Pesaḥ Frank zt"l, who was his grandfather's uncle, all those present sang the Shabbat zemirot together – men and women. In order to verify his memory from the days of his youth, he went back and asked Rabbi Frank's son, R. Avraham, and his wife, and they testified that indeed the women would sing, and their voices were heard, for they loved to sing aloud. And likewise Rabbi Dvir Azulai sent me testimony that the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rabbi Yitzḥak Yosef shlit"a wrote to him: "In the home of Maran my father and teacher it was the custom all the years that the whole family sings on Friday night and on the day together with the in-laws and all the brothers, and Maran told them that since the daughter does not sing 'solo', but her voice is swallowed up in the voices of everyone, there is no prohibition in this, even though her voice is also heard – that is, in a voice that does not dominate, but ordinary, and not at a high pitch," end quote. (Similarly he wrote in Yalkut Yosef, Shabbat part 1, vol. 3, pp. 368 to 373.)

sections.title_en: 13. Hearing Female Singers through Electronic Devices
sections.body_en:
Question: May one hear women's singing through electronic devices?

Answer: The poskim disagree about this, and the root of the doubt depends on the question of what the essence of the prohibition of hearing a woman's voice is: whether hearing a woman's singing voice is forbidden in itself because it may create an immodest atmosphere and thoughts of transgression – in which case there may be a prohibition also through an electronic device; or whether the concern is lest, out of hearing her singing voice, an excessive closeness be created between the woman who sings and the one who hears her, and thereby there is a concern that they will come to immodest situations and even to forbidden relations. There are three main views on this subject:

According to the first view, even hearing a woman's singing voice through an electronic device is forbidden, because the enjoyment of the voice of another woman is itself what is forbidden; therefore it makes no difference how her voice arrives, naturally or through an electronic device (Ḥelkat Yaakov OḤ 163; Shevet Ha-Levi 3:181; Az Nidberu vol. 6, 69:8).

According to the second view, there is no prohibition to hear a woman's singing voice when the listener does not see the singer and does not know her. For only hearing the singing of a woman one knows may arouse thoughts of transgression; but hearing the voice of a woman one does not know creates no closeness to any woman, and consequently does not cause impure thoughts, and there is no prohibition in it.5

According to the third view, the prohibition is only to hear a woman's natural singing voice and not the sound of a recording of her. However, when the hearing causes thoughts of transgression, it is forbidden, like anything that causes thoughts of transgression.

In practice, since the basis of the prohibition is from the words of the Sages, and it is a known rule that in a doubt concerning the words of the Sages one follows the lenient view, those who wish to be lenient and hear women's singing voices through an electronic device have on what to rely. And in principle, according to the lenient view it will also be permitted to watch women singing through an electronic device, for the prohibition is hearing a live performance and not a recording, which may even be from decades ago. And the less one knows the singer, or the longer ago the recording took place, the more agreed the permission is. However, when the watching arouses impure thoughts in the viewer, it is forbidden to him.6

notes_en.en: Those holding the second view, who permit hearing women's singing through the radio: Responsa Ma'arkhei Lev (Tzirelson, OḤ 5); Or Le-Tziyon (2, 6:13); Aseh Lekha Rav (1:28); Yabia Omer 1:6. And in Responsa Beit David (Leiter, 1:188) he wrote that the lenient have on what to rely, and so wrote Responsa Beit She'arim (OḤ 33) as a matter of law, but he wrote that it is ugly; and so wrote Mishneh Halakhot 5:224. In their view, one who has once seen the singer may not hear her voice through the radio. And in the view of Yabia Omer vol. 9, 108:43, even one who has seen her picture is permitted, and only one who knows her and is acquainted with her and has friendship with her is forbidden.

Some permitted hearing a woman's singing voice even for one who knows her personally, since it is not her voice but a voice coming out of a device like her voice. And so it is brought in Yabia Omer vol. 9, 108:43, from the book Yashiv Moshe (Torchin, p. 14) in the name of Rabbi Elyashiv. And so wrote Benei Banim (vol. 4, 7:6). Similarly it is brought in the name of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Halikhot Shlomo (Tefilla 20:12) that hearing a singing voice from a recording does not involve erva, but there is a concern of impure thoughts. And he wrote there that all this is in a recording, but if she is singing now, even though the hearing is through electrical devices, it is considered erva and forbidden. (There is room to say that perhaps some of the rabbis who were stringent about hearing from a device, as in the first view, or about one who had seen the singer's picture, as in the words of some of those holding the second view, were stringent when recordings were rare and there was in hearing them an aspect of breaching a fence. But in a situation where recordings have become common and pictures widespread, and some of them from many years ago, they would be lenient like Rabbi Elyashiv and Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach.)
This principle applies also to watching singing through the computer or the phone. For the basis of the prohibition is lest a connection be created between the listener and the singer, for many times they would usually sing together with wine, as is known from the prohibition of song (see Sota 48a; Gittin 7a; Tosafot there; and Rambam, Ta'aniyot 5:14); and since it concerns a recording, there is no possibility of reaching contact between the listener and the singer. And the more years pass, there are more recordings from past years, some of them of young singers who have become older, or older ones who have become elderly, and some are no longer alive, so that the watching is of an exhibit and not of a person. Therefore, as long as the watching does not cause thoughts of transgression, according to the lenient view there is no prohibition (on the definition of thoughts of transgression see Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 4:6).

sections.title_en: 14. A Reason for Modesty and for Covering the Hair
sections.body_en:
To explain the reason for women covering their hair, one must first say that the purpose of modesty is to turn beauty and natural love into something of deep and eternal meaning. And so that love will not be grasped only in its outward sides, halakha came and set bounds of modesty, which compel us to put the emphasis on the spiritual and soulful side of love; and out of this the natural outward beauty is revealed in its full depth and splendour.

Every woman must keep her modesty, but a married woman is doubly obligated in this. For as was said, love is not an outward thing that can be realised all at once in its entirety; rather there are layers of love, and the more modest a person is, the more he can develop spiritually and emotionally and reach the inner depths of love. By contrast, the love of one who is not bound by the rules of modesty tends to be outward and short, and after it reaches its peak it sinks and is lost. Go and see how many times immodest celebrities change their partners, and this after declaring openly that this time it is a true, pure and unique love that will last for ever and ever.

One who guides his life according to the halakhic rules of modesty becomes accustomed to relate to the physical sides with reverence and holy awe, because they express infinitely deep layers, of which outward beauty is one of the means of expression; and since outward beauty expresses things deeper than the sea, it should not be exposed before everyone.

The covering of the hair that accompanies marriage expresses the position that marriage is not the end of love nor its peak but only its beginning; and therefore it is precisely a married woman who must be all the more careful about her modesty, in order to preserve her beauty for the sake of deepening the bond between her and her husband, and in order to direct themselves to the revealing of the deep and wondrous layers of love.

sections.title_en: 15. General Rules of Covering the Hair
sections.body_en:
It is implied by the Talmud (Ketubot 72a) that the source for a married woman covering her hair is from the Torah, as it is said regarding a sota who sinned and was secluded with a strange man, that when she comes to bring her offering, as part of the punishment the Torah imposed on her, the kohen uncovers the hair of her head so that she will be ashamed, as it is said (Bamidbar 5:18): "And he shall uncover the head of the woman." From this it follows that according to the Torah the hair of a married woman must always be gathered (Meiri, Rashbatz and Riaz; and see Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:62). So is the view of most poskim, that the basis of the law of covering the hair is from the Torah; but by Torah law it is enough that the hair be gathered within a net or a small pouch, and the Sages added and established that all the hair must be covered with a kerchief that is not transparent. And some say that the whole law of gathering the hair and covering it is from the words of the Sages (Terumat Ha-Deshen 242, according to the view of the Rambam).

The law of covering the hair does not depend on custom; therefore even in a place where all the women are not careful to cover their hair, their custom does not change the law, and the obligation to cover the hair remains in force (MB 75:10).

The obligation to cover the hair applies to a married woman, but an unmarried woman need not cover her hair. And some say that from the aspect of the quality of modesty, unmarried women should take care not to go in the street with loose hair (MA 75:3). And indeed so some of the religious girls are accustomed, who gather the hair of their head with a band or braid their hair, so that it will not be loose. But many hold that there is no prohibition in this (Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel and Maginei Gibborim there). And since the basis of the dispute is in the words of the Sages, those who wish to be lenient may, according to the rule that in every doubt in the words of the Sages the halakha follows the lenient.

sections.title_en: 16. Must a Widow Cover Her Hair?
sections.body_en:
It was ruled in the 'Shulḥan Arukh' (EH 21:2): "The daughters of Israel shall not go with uncovered heads in the market, whether unmarried or married." And the commentators on the 'Shulḥan Arukh' explained that the intention is that widows and divorcees too must cover their hair, but young women who have not yet married need not cover their hair.

One of the great poskim of the last generation, Rabbi Moshe Feinstein zt"l, who lived and worked in America, was asked what a woman who was widowed and must support her children should do, when at the place where she can work they require her to come to work without a head covering. May she come to work without a head covering, or must she lose her livelihood in order to be careful about covering her hair? And he answered that although the obligation of a married woman to cover her hair has its source in the Written Torah, nevertheless a widow and a divorcee are not obligated in covering the hair by Torah law, and only by the words of the Sages or because of custom must they cover their hair. Therefore, so as not to lose her source of livelihood, she may be lenient and go at her place of work without a head covering (Igrot Moshe EH 1:57).

However, all this is possible abroad, among gentiles, when most people do not know the halakha and certainly are not bound by it. But in the Land it is not possible that an employer would demand of his employee that she not cover her hair; and if he asks, she must fight for her right to cover her hair according to halakha and not give in to his demand.

Sometimes there is a further need to be lenient, such as a young divorcee who fears that if she goes with a head covering she will have no chance of marrying again, because every young man who sees her will think that she is married and will not take an interest in her. And although she does not intend to lie and hide the fact that she is divorced, there is a chance that if she goes without a head covering, as young women are accustomed, a connection will develop with her, and afterwards, when she tells that she is divorced, the connection will continue; whereas if she goes with a head covering, the initial connection may not develop at all. And in such a case too Rabbi Feinstein permitted her to go without a head covering, because this is a very great need.

However, the permission is only when there is benefit from it; but a woman who belongs to Torah and Ḥaredi circles usually receives proposals through matchmaking. And if she removes her head covering, there is a concern that she will lessen her chance of receiving a proposal to her liking.

sections.title_en: 17. Saying Holy Words
sections.body_en:
We have already mentioned the saying of the Sages (Berakhot 24a): "Hair in a woman is erva." There are two meanings to their words: first, that every married woman must cover her hair; second, that if she does not cover her hair, men who see her may not say holy words.

In recent generations many women are not careful about covering the hair of their heads. This fact does not change the basic law, and the halakha obligating married women to cover their hair remains in its place. But the question is whether one may say holy words while seeing women without a head covering. This question arises, for example, at a wedding, where sometimes there are women around the ḥuppa who do not cover their hair, and the question is whether the rabbi conducting the ḥuppa may say the wedding blessings facing them. And likewise sometimes on Shabbat at the time of kiddush there are women present who do not cover their hair, and the question is whether one may say kiddush facing them.

Some say that even when many women are accustomed to go without a head covering, it is still forbidden to say holy words facing them. And if women who do not cover their hair stand facing the one conducting the ḥuppa, the one conducting the ḥuppa will have to close his eyes, or to fix his gaze on the siddur alone, and only in this way can he recite the wedding blessings (MB 75:10).

And some say that since people are accustomed to seeing women without a head covering, seeing them is not considered an exceptional thing that disturbs the concentration needed when saying holy words; therefore one may say holy words before them without needing to close one's eyes. And so rule many of the later poskim (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 75:7; Ben Ish Ḥai, Bo 12; Igrot Moshe OḤ 1:44).

It is important to note that in the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, this leniency was said only regarding hair; but regarding the covered places of a woman's body, even if all women become accustomed to go without sleeves and without skirts down to the knees, it will still be forbidden to say holy words before them. For there is a difference between the obligation to cover the hair of the head and covering the shok and the upper arm: the hair of the head only married women must cover, whereas the upper arm and the shok girls must cover already from a young age. Therefore, if women who do not cover their bodies according to halakha stand facing the one conducting the ḥuppa, he may not say the wedding blessings facing them, and he must turn his body in such a way that he does not see them. And if on all sides of him stand women who are not dressed according to halakha, in a pressing situation he may be lenient and close his eyes, or look into the siddur so that he does not see them at all, and so he can say the wedding blessings (SA OḤ 75:6; MB 29).

sections.title_en: 18. What Is the Measure of Covering the Hair?
sections.body_en:
Usually not all the hair goes under the kerchief or the hat; rather some of it is visible both at the front and at the back, and the question is whether this is permitted and proper.

It is implied by the Zohar that a woman should take care that not a single hair of the hair of her head be uncovered, and some wrote that so it is fitting to act (MA 75:2). But in the view of most poskim the halakha is not so, and it is clear that not all the hairs need be covered. And so wrote one of the great Rishonim, the Rashba (Berakhot 24a), that the hair that usually does not go under the kerchief involves no prohibition. And so ruled the Rema (OḤ 75:2). And some explained that this too is the intention of the Zohar, and all his words are about the hairs that are customarily covered according to halakha, that not even one of them may be seen.

In practice, there are two main approaches in defining this law. Some say that one should take care to cover all the hairs, but those hairs that, even after she tries to put them under the covering, naturally come out of the head covering – such as a little hair at the nape and at the temples – there is no obligation to cover (MB 75:14, and other poskim).

And some say that already from the period of the Mishna, the custom of covering the hair did not include all the hairs without exception. If so, there is no prohibition to uncover a little of the hair above the forehead or at the temples, because so is the custom of the worthy women in most of the diasporas under the Ishmaelites. And one should not be stringent and forbid it, for we find in many matters that the Sages were lenient so as not to impair a woman's beauty (Maharam Alashkar 35).

And so too Rabbi Feinstein ruled, that it is permitted for a little of the hairs above the forehead to be seen, and he set a bound for this: up to a square tefaḥ of the hair of the head a woman may uncover, and more than a tefaḥ is forbidden. And since the width of the face is about two tefaḥim, if a woman wants to uncover a little of the hair above her forehead, she will be permitted to uncover up to a measure of about half a tefaḥ, and one can measure half a tefaḥ by a measure of the width of two fingers, whose width is about four centimetres. In other words, since up to a square tefaḥ of her hair may be uncovered, a woman's head covering may reach to less than four centimetres from the edge of the hair at the forehead. For half a tefaḥ multiplied by two tefaḥim, which is roughly the width of the forehead, equals a square tefaḥ. And Rabbi Feinstein added that although ideally it is fitting to be stringent and cover all the hairs, nevertheless even a Torah scholar and God-fearing man should not refrain from marrying a woman who has good qualities and is careful about mitzvot and intends to uncover a little hair above the forehead, provided that she does not uncover more than the measure of the width of two fingers (Igrot Moshe EH 1:58).

sections.title_en: 19. Must a Woman Cover Her Hair in Her Home?
sections.body_en:
It is told in the Talmud (Yoma 47a) of a woman named Kimḥit, who merited to have seven righteous sons, all of whom served one after the other in the high priesthood. The Sages asked her: What did you do to merit this? She answered them: "In all my days the beams of my house never saw the braids of my hair." That is, I was very careful not to uncover the hair of my head even inside my home when I was alone. The Sages answered her: "Many did so and it did not help them." They meant to say that apparently she had further merits on account of which she merited such sons. In any case one can learn that it is a custom of piety for a woman to cover the hair of her head even when she is alone in her home.

But the poskim disagree on the question whether by law the obligation of covering the hair is only when the woman goes out of her home and courtyard, as the Tosafot hold (Ketubot 72b), or whether the obligation of covering the hair applies also inside the home, as is implied by the view of the Rambam. The 'Ḥatam Sofer' (OḤ 36) ruled that since the custom of women is to be stringent and cover their hair even in their room in their home, it is considered a complete law, and all women must cover their hair even inside their room. And also in the view of the 'Mishna Berura' (75:10) one should act so, and wear a head covering even inside the home.

And some disagree and are lenient; in their view, by law a woman may go inside her home without a head covering, provided that only the members of her household see her and not strangers. And so holds the author of the 'Igrot Moshe' (EH 1:58).

When going to sleep, according to all views one may be without a head covering.

sections.title_en: 20. A Wig
sections.body_en:
The poskim disagree on the question whether a woman may cover her hair with a wig. The root of the dispute depends on the question of what the basis of the prohibition of uncovering the hair of the head is: whether the main thing is the modest appearance that there is in covering the head, or whether specifically the hairs growing on her head express something intimate that a married woman must keep modestly hidden from strangers and reveal only before her husband.

In the view of the 'Shiltei Ha-Gibborim' and the Rema (SA OḤ 75:2), a married woman may wear a wig, because the wig hides her natural hairs. And although sometimes the hairs of the wig are more beautiful than her natural hair, the Sages did not forbid a woman to adorn herself with beautiful jewellery; rather the main thing is not to expose the personal sides outwardly, including the natural hairs, and likewise not to appear in a provocative manner. And if indeed the wig is beautiful and modest, in their view one may cover the hair with it.

By contrast, in the view of the author of the responsa 'Be'er Sheva' (siman 18) and the 'Sedei Ḥemed' and many other poskim, the basis of covering the hair is the modest appearance; therefore if one wears a wig, there is no added modesty in this relative to the original hair of the head, and therefore one may not cover the head with a wig.

In practice, the author of the 'Mishna Berura' mentioned the two views (75:15), and ruled on the basis of the 'Peri Megadim' that those who are accustomed to cover the head with a wig have on what to rely. But in places where women were accustomed not to wear a wig, one should be stringent, because of mar'it ayin (appearances).

And the Rishon Le-Tziyon, Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, wrote that according to the Sephardi custom there is a severe prohibition to wear a wig, because the wig is not considered a head covering (Yabia Omer vol. 4, 3:3; vol. 5, 5). However, several of the great Sephardi rabbis of the generation permitted wearing a wig, and among those who permit: the kabbalist Rabbi Ovadia Hadaya, author of the responsa 'Yaskil Avdi' (vol. 7, EH 16), the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu, and Rabbi Messas, Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem. If so, also among the Sephardi rabbis the matter is disputed; therefore also a woman who follows the Sephardi customs may be lenient and rely on the view that permits wearing a wig.

Rabbi Feinstein too wrote to a rabbi who wanted to forbid his wife to wear a wig, that although there are those who are stringent, most of our rabbis are lenient; therefore his honour cannot prevent his wife, the rabbanit, from wearing a wig, and although he wants to be stringent, he cannot impose his stringencies on her (Igrot Moshe EH vol. 2, 12. What he wrote in the name of most of our rabbis means those of Lithuania and Ashkenaz).

In practice many rabbis' wives are accustomed to be lenient and wear a wig. But most of the wives of the students of the Eretz-Yisrael yeshivot are accustomed to be stringent and cover their hair specifically with a kerchief or a hat and not with a wig. And some held that in the communities established by those students it is considered a binding custom, and as the 'Mishna Berura' ruled, one should not be lenient and wear a wig in a place where they were accustomed to be stringent, because of mar'it ayin. But in practice the whole Land is considered one place, and since there are many women in the Land who cover their hair with a wig, it cannot be said of any community in the Land that there is a binding custom to cover the head with a kerchief or a hat and not with a wig. Therefore one should not protest or comment to any woman who wishes to cover her hair with a wig, since there are many important and righteous women who act so.

sections.title_en: 21. Studying at a Mixed University
sections.body_en:
Question: Is there a permission to study at a university where men and women study together, when some of the female students and lecturers do not dress according to halakha?

Answer: Ideally one should study in a place where modesty is kept, where men study separately and women study separately. But when it is hard to study the desired profession in a modest place, one may be lenient and study at a mixed university, since it concerns a very great need. The need is great from the aspect of livelihood, from the aspect of a person's personal need to realise his talents in a field in which he is gifted and interested, from the aspect of the general public need that those who keep mitzvot be able to be active in all areas of life, and also so that they can be partners in the repair of the world. Therefore, as long as a person knows himself that he will not come to stumble in the prohibitions of forbidden relations, and will remain attached to Torah and mitzvot, he may study at a university.

The matter resembles a person who must go to a certain place, of whom it is explained in the Gemara that if there are two roads before him, on one of which there are women who are not dressed modestly, and on the second there are no immodest women, he must go on the good road; and if he chose to go on the road on which there are immodest women, he is wicked. And if there is only one road before him, and on it women who are not dressed modestly, he may go on it (Bava Batra 57b). And all that the Sages said, that a person should go on a road where there are no immodest women, applies where there is no significant difference between the two roads; but if the modest road is much longer, there is no obligation to go on it, and he is considered as one who has only one road before him (see Igrot Moshe EH 1:56).

And likewise regarding professional studies. One who can study in two places, in one of which there are problems of modesty and in the second not, is obligated to study in the proper place, even if for this he must lengthen his way a little or be a little flexible in his plans. But if the proper place is significantly far from his place of residence, or it is impossible to study there the profession he wants to study, and it is hard for him to compromise on studying another profession, he may study in a place where there are women who are not dressed according to halakha.

And so in practice we find merchants who sell their merchandise to women who are not modest, and likewise clerks who work in places to which women who are not modest come, and no one raises before religious merchants and clerks a demand to refrain from selling to or serving women who are not modest. And likewise no one demands of a person to refrain from going to offices where the clerks are dressed immodestly. For when there is a great need, there is no prohibition. However, when a person knows himself that through this he may stumble in the prohibitions of forbidden relations, he may not put himself into the test.7

In any case, even when there is a permission to study in these places, one must strive to reduce the risks. First, it is right to come to these institutions after marriage. In addition, the student should strengthen himself by fixing times for Torah and prayers with a minyan. Likewise it is fitting that he strengthen himself through a religious outward appearance, including a kippa that covers most of the head and wearing the tzitzit out, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39): "And you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them, and you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes." And likewise it is very important that the student be connected to a religious community and to religious friends. In addition, beyond polite and courteous behaviour, one should avoid becoming absorbed in the mixed society, and keep a respectful and distant relationship with the women who study with him.

notes_en.en: The value of studying the sciences and the value of livelihood are considered a very great need that cannot be harmed because of thoughts of transgression, just as young men are not obligated to marry at the age of thirteen in order to be saved from thoughts of transgression (see Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 4:7, notes 11-12). One can say that preventing Jews from the possibility of engaging in science and an honourable livelihood constitutes a real danger to the existence of the Jewish people. However, forbidden relations themselves override everything, and about them it was said: be killed rather than transgress. And even when there is a concern of forbidden relations, as long as the concern is reasonable, it is better to give up livelihood and the study of science, provided that one does not enter a concern of forbidden relations. (On the definition of thoughts of transgression see Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 4:6.)

sections.title_en: 22. Physiotherapy Studies
sections.body_en:
Question: May students of the physiotherapy department practise massage, men on women and women on men? According to the heads of the department, it is necessary to practise on members of the opposite sex, since there are differences between the sexes, and one who does not practise this will not be able to receive proper training as a physiotherapist.

Answer: It is forbidden to practise massage of men on women and women on men, and in a place that requires this it is forbidden to study. Admittedly, in order to treat a patient a doctor or a physiotherapist may touch a member of the opposite sex and see private places on his body. And ideally, even for a medical need, since physiotherapy treatment is a prolonged treatment, it is better that a man treat men and a woman women. But regarding study there is no permission. And one should not accept the claim of the heads of the department, who claim that in order to train them properly they must also practise on members of the opposite sex, for according to the opinion of experts there are no significant differences in this respect between the body of a man and of a woman. Not only this, but only recently have men begun to enter this profession, and before that only women studied physiotherapy, and no one claimed then that they must practise on men (according to Rabbi Prof. Avraham Steinberg, author of the Encyclopedia of Jewish Medical Ethics).
